repository.description: Self-hosted web console for machines behind NAT and firewalls: one outbound reverse SSH tunnel per device gives you a browser terminal, files, RDP / VNC / RustDesk desktops, a remote browser and the LAN behind it — shared with fine-grained permissions and scriptable through a CLI, REST API and MCP. Rust + Next.js.
repository.name: telepy
repository.readme:
English | 繁體中文 | 日本語

Telepy is a self-hosted web console for machines you can't reach directly: servers behind NAT, a Raspberry Pi at home, an office PC behind a firewall, an OpenWrt router. Each device dials out **one reverse SSH tunnel** to your Telepy server, and from then on you work on it from the browser — terminal, files, remote desktop, a browser that goes online through the device, and the machines on its LAN. Share devices with teammates under fine-grained permissions, and script everything with the `telepy` command line, the REST API or MCP. Nothing is opened or installed on the device's network beyond that one outbound SSH connection. ![The tunnels page: health, latency, how each device connects, public and LAN addresses, OS, labels, who is connected](./docs/screenshots/en/tunnels.png) ## What you can do ### Connect devices - **One command on Linux, macOS and OpenWrt.** Paste a `curl … | sudo sh` line on the device: the script works out what the device has (shell, HTTP tool, OpenSSH or Dropbear, systemd / launchd / procd), creates the tunnel key, registers the device, authorizes Telepy, pins Telepy's host key, installs a service and waits until Telepy has logged in through the tunnel; `--check` runs the checks alone first. For everything else (Windows, Docker, appliances) a five-step wizard generates SSH, AutoSSH, systemd, PowerShell, Docker run and Docker Compose scripts. - **The SSH port, or the web port when that is all that gets out.** Devices try the gateway's SSH port first and carry SSH inside a WebSocket on the web port when it is blocked. Every tunnel shows how it connects (SSH or SSH over WSS), and an installed device can be switched to the automatic way without dropping its tunnel. When your web name sits behind a proxy that only carries web traffic, give SSH a name of its own. - **Tidy installs on the device.** Each tunnel's service gets a private install name; Telepy shows what is installed where, renames older installs and removes extra copies, all without taking the device offline. - **Health at a glance.** Online / degraded / offline / never connected, per-hop latency, uptime and connection history, the device's public and LAN addresses with IP-change alerts, and daily device facts (OS, memory, disk, load, pending reboot) with warnings. - **Organize hundreds of devices.** A dense list or cards, labels, pins, personal groups, and a search with filters such as `status:down`, `label:env=prod`, `os:openwrt` or `lastseen:>1d`. ### Work on a device - **Web terminal** with tabs, Nerd Fonts, built-in and custom colour schemes, shells that survive a dropped connection (when you allow it), session recording, commands kept out of the device's shell history (if you want), and a **toolbox** of saved command snippets with variables. - **File manager** over SFTP: drag-and-drop uploads, move / copy / rename / delete / permissions, zip downloads, image preview and an in-browser editor that never leaves half a file. - **Remote desktop** in the browser: RDP and VNC through the tunnel (guacd), or RustDesk decoded in the tab, with sound, clipboard control, file transfer, multi-monitor cropping, and scaling and a resolution that follow your window. - **Remote browser:** a real Chromium (KasmVNC) whose traffic leaves through the device, for web consoles that only answer on the device's network. - **Network topology:** scan a device's LAN without installing anything, see vendors and open ports, then open a terminal or desktop on a LAN host through the device, or copy an `ssh -J` / `ProxyJump` setup. - **From your own computer:** one command adds every device to `~/.ssh/config` (each device's host key checked too), the command sheet gives copy-ready `ssh -L` / `-R` / `-D` / `-J`, `scp` and `rsync` lines, and the **SSH config editor** shows what every host in your config really uses, fixes lines that never take effect and simplifies the file — every change checked against how ssh reads it (`telepy config tidy` does the same in a terminal). ### Teams and control - **Sharing** with VIEW / EDIT / ADMIN permissions, per-account allow-lists, shares that expire, and access requests for temporary extra rights. Taking access away ends that person's open sessions at once. - **Feature permissions and user groups:** decide who may use the terminal, files, desktop, LAN discovery, API tokens, MCP apps and more — for everyone, a group or one person. - **Command rules:** block commands, hold them for approval or show a reminder — your own rules for the devices you manage, plus site-wide rules that admins may let people switch off on their own devices — in the web terminal and for MCP agents alike. - **Live sessions:** see who is connected where, watch a terminal live (and hand over the keyboard), or end a session. - **Sign-in security:** passkeys and authenticator apps, a second-factor check before sensitive devices, a list of your signed-in browsers, new-device alerts, and an optional discreet sign-in page. - **Notifications:** in-app and desktop notifications per event, with site defaults admins can enforce and mutes per device; webhooks to Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Teams, Telegram, ntfy or your own service, personal or site-wide. - **Audit:** tamper-evident logs (hash chains), terminal recordings and sign-in history. - **Server health:** the admin section runs the server's own checks on the live server — configuration, keys, companion services, how visitors' addresses arrive, the audit chain — next to live numbers, and lets you acknowledge a known problem. ### Automate - **`telepy` command line:** `telepy ls`, `telepy ssh web-01`, `telepy exec --label env=prod -- uptime`, `telepy cp`, live sessions, recordings, snippets, LAN hosts and scripted browsers; `ssh` / `scp` / `sftp` go through the web port, and `telepy update` keeps the CLI current. - **REST API** with personal API tokens (scopes, tunnel limits, expiry, a call log) and a generated OpenAPI document. - **MCP server** for AI agents (Claude Code, Cursor, …): approved per app through OAuth, every tool call audited, command rules and permissions applied. ## Screenshots

Web terminal + file manager — tabs, the SFTP side panel and the latency of each hop.
Network — the LAN behind a device, scanned through its own sshd, with vendors and open ports.

Remote desktop — a VNC desktop through the tunnel, with stream stats and screen selection.
Remote browser — Chromium that goes online through the device.

Add a device — one command; the page shows what the script does and follows it until Telepy has logged in.
Command rules — your own and site-wide rules: block, approve, remind or allow, with a tester that shows who would be asked.

Live sessions — who is connected, from where; watch or end a session.
Feature permissions — per person, per user group or for everyone.

SSH config editor — paste a ~/.ssh/config, see what each host uses and simplify it, checked against how ssh reads it.
Server health — the server's own checks, live numbers and the last 24 hours.

API — personal tokens with scopes, tunnel limits and a per-token call summary.
Agent activity — every MCP tool call, including commands waiting for approval.
## How it works ``` your browser ──https──▶ Traefik ──▶ frontend (Next.js) │ └──────▶ backend (Rust) ◀══ reverse SSH (outbound from the device) ══ device ── LAN hosts │ REST API · WebSockets · built-in SSH gateway · monitor ├──▶ kasm-browser (Chromium for remote browsing) └──▶ guacd (RDP / VNC) ``` A device runs `ssh -R 0:localhost:22 telepy@` — straight to the gateway's SSH port, or inside a WebSocket on the web port when only HTTPS gets out (the join script and the generated scripts set this up as a service). The backend's built-in SSH gateway accepts it, recognises the tunnel by its key and keeps the forward in memory — nothing is bound on the host. Everything Telepy does on the device — terminal, files, desktop, remote browser, LAN scans — opens a channel inside that one connection and logs in to the device's own sshd with that tunnel's service key. The device needs no public IP and no inbound firewall rule; Telepy pins each device's host key, and the device pins Telepy's. More diagrams of what happens inside — joining a device, the terminal, files, remote desktop, sharing, command rules, keys, notifications, the CLI and server health — are in **[Telepy in pictures](./docs/visual-guide.md)**. Telepy runs as five containers: | Service | Role | | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `traefik` | Reverse proxy: `/api/*`, `/ws/*` (devices' WebSocket way in too), `/mcp` and OAuth discovery go to the backend, everything else to the frontend | | `frontend` | Next.js web UI | | `backend` | One Rust process (axum + russh): REST API, WebSockets, the SSH gateway, monitoring, SQLite | | `kasm-browser` | KasmVNC + Chromium for remote browser sessions | | `guacd` | Apache Guacamole's RDP / VNC engine for remote desktops (internal network only) | ## Quick start Requires Docker with the Compose plugin. 1. Create the environment file and set at least `SECRET_KEY`, `INTERNAL_API_TOKEN` and `SERVER_DOMAIN` (the public address behind an HTTPS proxy can go in `PUBLIC_URL` or, later, **Site settings → Server**): ```bash cp .env.example .env ``` 2. Build and start the stack. On its first start the backend creates the gateway's host keys and its service key under `ssh/` (keys that already exist are kept — devices pin them): ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` 3. Check it. The admin section's **Server health** page runs every check once you are signed in; the same checks are available from the command line: ```bash docker compose exec backend telepy-server doctor ``` 4. Open `http://localhost:` (default `http://localhost:8787`) and sign in. > [!NOTE] > The **first account** becomes the administrator — whether it signs in with Google or is created with > `docker compose exec backend telepy-server create-superuser --username admin --password …`. For production, put an HTTPS proxy in front of Traefik, set the public address, and make the gateway port (`REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT`) reachable for your devices. If the web name goes through a proxy that only carries web traffic (Cloudflare's orange cloud, a CDN, an HTTP load balancer), give SSH a name that points straight at the server under **Site settings → Server → SSH host** — or let devices use the web port. Visitors' addresses (sign-in history, live sessions) come through X-Forwarded-For; by default every internal proxy in front of the backend is skipped automatically. **Server health** in the admin section checks the whole setup and shows how the address of your own request was worked out. ### Connect a device - **Linux / macOS / OpenWrt:** **Tunnels → Create Tunnel → One command**, copy the command and run it on the device. The page follows each step and turns green once Telepy has logged in through the tunnel. Details: [docs/device-join.md](./docs/device-join.md). - **Anything else (Windows, Docker, appliances):** **Step by step** — paste the device's public key, choose the login accounts, authorize Telepy's key, run one of the generated scripts, and verify the login. When the tunnel is **Online**, the terminal, files, desktop and browser buttons on its card are ready. ## Configuration These values live in `.env` because the stack needs them before it starts (see [`.env.example`](./.env.example) for the full comments): | Variable | Default | Description | | ------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `PROJECT_NAME` | `main` | Suffix of container and network names (one per stack on a host) | | `DEBUG` | `false` | Debug logging | | `WEB_SERVER_PORT` | `8787` | Port Traefik publishes for the web UI, API and WebSockets | | `REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT` | `24242` | Port devices dial for their reverse SSH tunnel | | `SERVER_DOMAIN` | `localhost` | Host name of this server; written into scripts, SSH configs and pinned host keys | | `SECRET_KEY` | — | Signs sign-ins and seals stored secrets; set a long random value before real use | | `INTERNAL_API_TOKEN` | — | Secret between the backend and the kasm-browser container | | `GEOIP_DIR` / `OUI_DIR` | `/data/geoip` / `/data/oui` | Where the backend reads the IP geolocation databases and the NIC vendor list (paths inside the container; `telepy-server geoip` / `oui` fill them) | The next ones are **optional**: each is also a field under **Site settings → Server**, which an admin can change in the web without a restart. Leave the variable empty to manage it there; a value in `.env` wins and locks that field. | Variable | Site setting | When empty | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `PUBLIC_URL` | Public address | Taken from the request (OAuth issuer, passkey origin, join URL) | | `SSH_SERVER_DOMAIN` | SSH host | Same as `SERVER_DOMAIN`; set it when the web name goes through a web-only proxy | | `SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` | Google client ID | No Google sign-in | | `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` | Trusted proxies | `auto`: every internal address in X-Forwarded-For is a proxy | | `CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | Client IP header | None (Cloudflare's header is used when the request came through Cloudflare) | | `GATEWAY_PROXY_PROTOCOL_FROM` | PROXY protocol sources for the SSH gateway | Off | | `DEVICE_PROBE` | Daily device check | On: a daily read-only login for each device's addresses and facts | | `KEEP_SHARED_SERVICE_KEY` | Keep the shared service key on devices | Off | | `LOG_LEVEL` | Log level | `info` (`debug` with `DEBUG=true`) | | `OPENAPI_ENABLED` | API reference | On (Swagger UI and the OpenAPI document, signed-in users only) | Everything else — registration, sign-in lifetimes and two-factor requirements, remote browser and desktop limits, MCP sessions, webhooks, notifications, terminal and command-rule defaults — is a site setting too, and users and feature permissions are in the admin section (**Users & access**). ## Command line, API and MCP **`telepy` CLI** — install a release build (macOS, Linux, Windows; every Telepy release carries one) or `cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/NatLee/telepy telepy-cli`. The web's **CLI** page (sidebar Developers → CLI) has the install command for your computer and examples filled in with your own tunnels: ```sh telepy login https://telepy.example.com # browser sign-in, or --token tpt_… from the API page telepy ls # tunnels with health, latency, accounts and labels telepy ssh web-01 # your system ssh through the tunnel, Telepy's host key pinned telepy exec --label env=prod -- uptime # many devices at once; command rules and audit apply telepy cp ./app.conf web-01:/etc/app/ telepy config tidy # simplify ~/.ssh/config, checked against how ssh reads it telepy api activity --follow # every call your API tokens make, as it happens telepy update # replace this binary with the latest release ``` In CI set `TELEPY_URL` and `TELEPY_TOKEN` instead of signing in. Details: [docs/cli.md](./docs/cli.md). **REST API** — create a personal token on the **API** page; it lists every endpoint a token may call, with `curl` examples. The OpenAPI document is at `/api/openapi.json` and Swagger UI at `/api/__hidden_swagger` (both need a sign-in; `telepy-server openapi` prints the document). **MCP** — point an MCP client at `https:///mcp`, e.g. `claude mcp add --transport http telepy https:///mcp`. The first use opens an approval page where you pick the permissions and tunnels; the **MCP** page has the setup for each client. Details: [docs/mcp.md](./docs/mcp.md). ## Maintenance Every maintenance task is a `telepy-server` command inside the backend container, so it is the same on Linux, macOS and Windows: | Command | What it does | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server doctor` | Check the keys, database, configuration and companion services (exit 1 on a problem) | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server create-superuser --username --password ` | Create an administrator account | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server keygen` | Create missing gateway host keys and the service key (also done at every start; existing keys are kept) | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server geoip` | Download offline IP geolocation (DB-IP Lite), then restart the backend; re-run monthly | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server oui` | Download the IEEE vendor list so LAN hosts show their NIC vendor, then restart the backend | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server migrate` | Reconcile the database schema (also runs on every start) | | `docker compose logs -f backend` | Follow the backend's logs | Upgrading is `git pull && docker compose up -d --build`; the database schema is reconciled on start. ## Documentation - **[Telepy in pictures](./docs/visual-guide.md)** — the app's diagrams and a few recordings, feature by feature - [All documentation](./docs/README.md) — every document below, in English, 繁體中文 and 日本語 - [The `telepy` command line and API tokens](./docs/cli.md) - [MCP: AI agents on your devices](./docs/mcp.md) - [Webhooks: events, formats and signatures](./docs/webhooks.md) - [One-command device join (Linux, macOS, OpenWrt)](./docs/device-join.md) - [Remote desktop (RDP / VNC / RustDesk)](./docs/remote-desktop.md) - [Remote browser (KasmVNC)](./docs/remote-browser.md) - [How the backend reaches devices](./docs/device-connections.md) - [Latency measurement deep dive](./docs/latency-deep-dive.md) - [Rust backend migration plan](./docs/engineering/rust-migration-plan.md) (Traditional Chinese) and [benchmark: Django vs Rust](./docs/benchmarks.md) - [How the README screenshots are made](./docs/screenshots/README.md) - [Articles](./docs/engineering/articles/) (Traditional Chinese) - Release notes: [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/NatLee/telepy/releases) ## Contributors

Nat Lee
H. Alice
Boris Lok

Telepy is a self-hosted web console for machines you can't reach directly: servers behind NAT, a Raspberry Pi at home, an office PC behind a firewall, an OpenWrt router. Each device dials out **one reverse SSH tunnel** to your Telepy server, and from then on you work on it from the browser — terminal, files, remote desktop, a browser that goes online through the device, and the machines on its LAN. Share devices with teammates under fine-grained permissions, and script everything with the `telepy` command line, the REST API or MCP. Nothing is opened or installed on the device's network beyond that one outbound SSH connection. ![The tunnels page: health, latency, how each device connects, public and LAN addresses, OS, labels, who is connected](./docs/screenshots/en/tunnels.png) ## What you can do ### Connect devices - **One command on Linux, macOS and OpenWrt.** Paste a `curl … | sudo sh` line on the device: the script works out what the device has (shell, HTTP tool, OpenSSH or Dropbear, systemd / launchd / procd), creates the tunnel key, registers the device, authorizes Telepy, pins Telepy's host key, installs a service and waits until Telepy has logged in through the tunnel; `--check` runs the checks alone first. For everything else (Windows, Docker, appliances) a five-step wizard generates SSH, AutoSSH, systemd, PowerShell, Docker run and Docker Compose scripts. - **The SSH port, or the web port when that is all that gets out.** Devices try the gateway's SSH port first and carry SSH inside a WebSocket on the web port when it is blocked. Every tunnel shows how it connects (SSH or SSH over WSS), and an installed device can be switched to the automatic way without dropping its tunnel. When your web name sits behind a proxy that only carries web traffic, give SSH a name of its own. - **Tidy installs on the device.** Each tunnel's service gets a private install name; Telepy shows what is installed where, renames older installs and removes extra copies, all without taking the device offline. - **Health at a glance.** Online / degraded / offline / never connected, per-hop latency, uptime and connection history, the device's public and LAN addresses with IP-change alerts, and daily device facts (OS, memory, disk, load, pending reboot) with warnings. - **Organize hundreds of devices.** A dense list or cards, labels, pins, personal groups, and a search with filters such as `status:down`, `label:env=prod`, `os:openwrt` or `lastseen:>1d`. ### Work on a device - **Web terminal** with tabs, Nerd Fonts, built-in and custom colour schemes, shells that survive a dropped connection (when you allow it), session recording, commands kept out of the device's shell history (if you want), and a **toolbox** of saved command snippets with variables. - **File manager** over SFTP: drag-and-drop uploads, move / copy / rename / delete / permissions, zip downloads, image preview and an in-browser editor that never leaves half a file. - **Remote desktop** in the browser: RDP and VNC through the tunnel (guacd), or RustDesk decoded in the tab, with sound, clipboard control, file transfer, multi-monitor cropping, and scaling and a resolution that follow your window. - **Remote browser:** a real Chromium (KasmVNC) whose traffic leaves through the device, for web consoles that only answer on the device's network. - **Network topology:** scan a device's LAN without installing anything, see vendors and open ports, then open a terminal or desktop on a LAN host through the device, or copy an `ssh -J` / `ProxyJump` setup. - **From your own computer:** one command adds every device to `~/.ssh/config` (each device's host key checked too), the command sheet gives copy-ready `ssh -L` / `-R` / `-D` / `-J`, `scp` and `rsync` lines, and the **SSH config editor** shows what every host in your config really uses, fixes lines that never take effect and simplifies the file — every change checked against how ssh reads it (`telepy config tidy` does the same in a terminal). ### Teams and control - **Sharing** with VIEW / EDIT / ADMIN permissions, per-account allow-lists, shares that expire, and access requests for temporary extra rights. Taking access away ends that person's open sessions at once. - **Feature permissions and user groups:** decide who may use the terminal, files, desktop, LAN discovery, API tokens, MCP apps and more — for everyone, a group or one person. - **Command rules:** block commands, hold them for approval or show a reminder — your own rules for the devices you manage, plus site-wide rules that admins may let people switch off on their own devices — in the web terminal and for MCP agents alike. - **Live sessions:** see who is connected where, watch a terminal live (and hand over the keyboard), or end a session. - **Sign-in security:** passkeys and authenticator apps, a second-factor check before sensitive devices, a list of your signed-in browsers, new-device alerts, and an optional discreet sign-in page. - **Notifications:** in-app and desktop notifications per event, with site defaults admins can enforce and mutes per device; webhooks to Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Teams, Telegram, ntfy or your own service, personal or site-wide. - **Audit:** tamper-evident logs (hash chains), terminal recordings and sign-in history. - **Server health:** the admin section runs the server's own checks on the live server — configuration, keys, companion services, how visitors' addresses arrive, the audit chain — next to live numbers, and lets you acknowledge a known problem. ### Automate - **`telepy` command line:** `telepy ls`, `telepy ssh web-01`, `telepy exec --label env=prod -- uptime`, `telepy cp`, live sessions, recordings, snippets, LAN hosts and scripted browsers; `ssh` / `scp` / `sftp` go through the web port, and `telepy update` keeps the CLI current. - **REST API** with personal API tokens (scopes, tunnel limits, expiry, a call log) and a generated OpenAPI document. - **MCP server** for AI agents (Claude Code, Cursor, …): approved per app through OAuth, every tool call audited, command rules and permissions applied. ## Screenshots

Web terminal + file manager — tabs, the SFTP side panel and the latency of each hop.
Network — the LAN behind a device, scanned through its own sshd, with vendors and open ports.

Remote desktop — a VNC desktop through the tunnel, with stream stats and screen selection.
Remote browser — Chromium that goes online through the device.

Add a device — one command; the page shows what the script does and follows it until Telepy has logged in.
Command rules — your own and site-wide rules: block, approve, remind or allow, with a tester that shows who would be asked.

Live sessions — who is connected, from where; watch or end a session.
Feature permissions — per person, per user group or for everyone.

SSH config editor — paste a ~/.ssh/config, see what each host uses and simplify it, checked against how ssh reads it.
Server health — the server's own checks, live numbers and the last 24 hours.

API — personal tokens with scopes, tunnel limits and a per-token call summary.
Agent activity — every MCP tool call, including commands waiting for approval.
## How it works ``` your browser ──https──▶ Traefik ──▶ frontend (Next.js) │ └──────▶ backend (Rust) ◀══ reverse SSH (outbound from the device) ══ device ── LAN hosts │ REST API · WebSockets · built-in SSH gateway · monitor ├──▶ kasm-browser (Chromium for remote browsing) └──▶ guacd (RDP / VNC) ``` A device runs `ssh -R 0:localhost:22 telepy@` — straight to the gateway's SSH port, or inside a WebSocket on the web port when only HTTPS gets out (the join script and the generated scripts set this up as a service). The backend's built-in SSH gateway accepts it, recognises the tunnel by its key and keeps the forward in memory — nothing is bound on the host. Everything Telepy does on the device — terminal, files, desktop, remote browser, LAN scans — opens a channel inside that one connection and logs in to the device's own sshd with that tunnel's service key. The device needs no public IP and no inbound firewall rule; Telepy pins each device's host key, and the device pins Telepy's. More diagrams of what happens inside — joining a device, the terminal, files, remote desktop, sharing, command rules, keys, notifications, the CLI and server health — are in **[Telepy in pictures](./docs/visual-guide.md)**. Telepy runs as five containers: | Service | Role | | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `traefik` | Reverse proxy: `/api/*`, `/ws/*` (devices' WebSocket way in too), `/mcp` and OAuth discovery go to the backend, everything else to the frontend | | `frontend` | Next.js web UI | | `backend` | One Rust process (axum + russh): REST API, WebSockets, the SSH gateway, monitoring, SQLite | | `kasm-browser` | KasmVNC + Chromium for remote browser sessions | | `guacd` | Apache Guacamole's RDP / VNC engine for remote desktops (internal network only) | ## Quick start Requires Docker with the Compose plugin. 1. Create the environment file and set at least `SECRET_KEY`, `INTERNAL_API_TOKEN` and `SERVER_DOMAIN` (the public address behind an HTTPS proxy can go in `PUBLIC_URL` or, later, **Site settings → Server**): ```bash cp .env.example .env ``` 2. Build and start the stack. On its first start the backend creates the gateway's host keys and its service key under `ssh/` (keys that already exist are kept — devices pin them): ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` 3. Check it. The admin section's **Server health** page runs every check once you are signed in; the same checks are available from the command line: ```bash docker compose exec backend telepy-server doctor ``` 4. Open `http://localhost:` (default `http://localhost:8787`) and sign in. > [!NOTE] > The **first account** becomes the administrator — whether it signs in with Google or is created with > `docker compose exec backend telepy-server create-superuser --username admin --password …`. For production, put an HTTPS proxy in front of Traefik, set the public address, and make the gateway port (`REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT`) reachable for your devices. If the web name goes through a proxy that only carries web traffic (Cloudflare's orange cloud, a CDN, an HTTP load balancer), give SSH a name that points straight at the server under **Site settings → Server → SSH host** — or let devices use the web port. Visitors' addresses (sign-in history, live sessions) come through X-Forwarded-For; by default every internal proxy in front of the backend is skipped automatically. **Server health** in the admin section checks the whole setup and shows how the address of your own request was worked out. ### Connect a device - **Linux / macOS / OpenWrt:** **Tunnels → Create Tunnel → One command**, copy the command and run it on the device. The page follows each step and turns green once Telepy has logged in through the tunnel. Details: [docs/device-join.md](./docs/device-join.md). - **Anything else (Windows, Docker, appliances):** **Step by step** — paste the device's public key, choose the login accounts, authorize Telepy's key, run one of the generated scripts, and verify the login. When the tunnel is **Online**, the terminal, files, desktop and browser buttons on its card are ready. ## Configuration These values live in `.env` because the stack needs them before it starts (see [`.env.example`](./.env.example) for the full comments): | Variable | Default | Description | | ------------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `PROJECT_NAME` | `main` | Suffix of container and network names (one per stack on a host) | | `DEBUG` | `false` | Debug logging | | `WEB_SERVER_PORT` | `8787` | Port Traefik publishes for the web UI, API and WebSockets | | `REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT` | `24242` | Port devices dial for their reverse SSH tunnel | | `SERVER_DOMAIN` | `localhost` | Host name of this server; written into scripts, SSH configs and pinned host keys | | `SECRET_KEY` | — | Signs sign-ins and seals stored secrets; set a long random value before real use | | `INTERNAL_API_TOKEN` | — | Secret between the backend and the kasm-browser container | | `GEOIP_DIR` / `OUI_DIR` | `/data/geoip` / `/data/oui` | Where the backend reads the IP geolocation databases and the NIC vendor list (paths inside the container; `telepy-server geoip` / `oui` fill them) | The next ones are **optional**: each is also a field under **Site settings → Server**, which an admin can change in the web without a restart. Leave the variable empty to manage it there; a value in `.env` wins and locks that field. | Variable | Site setting | When empty | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `PUBLIC_URL` | Public address | Taken from the request (OAuth issuer, passkey origin, join URL) | | `SSH_SERVER_DOMAIN` | SSH host | Same as `SERVER_DOMAIN`; set it when the web name goes through a web-only proxy | | `SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` | Google client ID | No Google sign-in | | `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` | Trusted proxies | `auto`: every internal address in X-Forwarded-For is a proxy | | `CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | Client IP header | None (Cloudflare's header is used when the request came through Cloudflare) | | `GATEWAY_PROXY_PROTOCOL_FROM` | PROXY protocol sources for the SSH gateway | Off | | `DEVICE_PROBE` | Daily device check | On: a daily read-only login for each device's addresses and facts | | `KEEP_SHARED_SERVICE_KEY` | Keep the shared service key on devices | Off | | `LOG_LEVEL` | Log level | `info` (`debug` with `DEBUG=true`) | | `OPENAPI_ENABLED` | API reference | On (Swagger UI and the OpenAPI document, signed-in users only) | Everything else — registration, sign-in lifetimes and two-factor requirements, remote browser and desktop limits, MCP sessions, webhooks, notifications, terminal and command-rule defaults — is a site setting too, and users and feature permissions are in the admin section (**Users & access**). ## Command line, API and MCP **`telepy` CLI** — install a release build (macOS, Linux, Windows; every Telepy release carries one) or `cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/NatLee/telepy telepy-cli`. The web's **CLI** page (sidebar Developers → CLI) has the install command for your computer and examples filled in with your own tunnels: ```sh telepy login https://telepy.example.com # browser sign-in, or --token tpt_… from the API page telepy ls # tunnels with health, latency, accounts and labels telepy ssh web-01 # your system ssh through the tunnel, Telepy's host key pinned telepy exec --label env=prod -- uptime # many devices at once; command rules and audit apply telepy cp ./app.conf web-01:/etc/app/ telepy config tidy # simplify ~/.ssh/config, checked against how ssh reads it telepy api activity --follow # every call your API tokens make, as it happens telepy update # replace this binary with the latest release ``` In CI set `TELEPY_URL` and `TELEPY_TOKEN` instead of signing in. Details: [docs/cli.md](./docs/cli.md). **REST API** — create a personal token on the **API** page; it lists every endpoint a token may call, with `curl` examples. The OpenAPI document is at `/api/openapi.json` and Swagger UI at `/api/__hidden_swagger` (both need a sign-in; `telepy-server openapi` prints the document). **MCP** — point an MCP client at `https:///mcp`, e.g. `claude mcp add --transport http telepy https:///mcp`. The first use opens an approval page where you pick the permissions and tunnels; the **MCP** page has the setup for each client. Details: [docs/mcp.md](./docs/mcp.md). ## Maintenance Every maintenance task is a `telepy-server` command inside the backend container, so it is the same on Linux, macOS and Windows: | Command | What it does | | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server doctor` | Check the keys, database, configuration and companion services (exit 1 on a problem) | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server create-superuser --username --password ` | Create an administrator account | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server keygen` | Create missing gateway host keys and the service key (also done at every start; existing keys are kept) | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server geoip` | Download offline IP geolocation (DB-IP Lite), then restart the backend; re-run monthly | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server oui` | Download the IEEE vendor list so LAN hosts show their NIC vendor, then restart the backend | | `docker compose exec backend telepy-server migrate` | Reconcile the database schema (also runs on every start) | | `docker compose logs -f backend` | Follow the backend's logs | Upgrading is `git pull && docker compose up -d --build`; the database schema is reconciled on start. ## Documentation - **[Telepy in pictures](./docs/visual-guide.md)** — the app's diagrams and a few recordings, feature by feature - [All documentation](./docs/README.md) — every document below, in English, 繁體中文 and 日本語 - [The `telepy` command line and API tokens](./docs/cli.md) - [MCP: AI agents on your devices](./docs/mcp.md) - [Webhooks: events, formats and signatures](./docs/webhooks.md) - [One-command device join (Linux, macOS, OpenWrt)](./docs/device-join.md) - [Remote desktop (RDP / VNC / RustDesk)](./docs/remote-desktop.md) - [Remote browser (KasmVNC)](./docs/remote-browser.md) - [How the backend reaches devices](./docs/device-connections.md) - [Latency measurement deep dive](./docs/latency-deep-dive.md) - [Rust backend migration plan](./docs/engineering/rust-migration-plan.md) (Traditional Chinese) and [benchmark: Django vs Rust](./docs/benchmarks.md) - [How the README screenshots are made](./docs/screenshots/README.md) - [Articles](./docs/engineering/articles/) (Traditional Chinese) - Release notes: [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/NatLee/telepy/releases) ## Contributors

sampled_files.docker-compose.yml:
x-common-networks: &common-networks
  networks:
    - telepy-network

x-common-restart: &common-restart
  restart: always

services:

  traefik:
    <<: [ *common-networks, *common-restart ]
    # v3.0.x 世代有多個 WebSocket 相關修正（rc 期間曾有 60s 斷線 bug）；升到目前穩定版，
    # 並搭配 traefik.yml 的 readTimeout: 0（v3 預設 60s 會切長連線）。
    # The v3.0.x era shipped several WebSocket fixes; pin current stable and pair with
    # readTimeout: 0 in traefik.yml (the v3 default of 60s kills long-lived connections).
    image: traefik:v3.7.6
    container_name: telepy-traefik-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    command:
      - "--configFile=/etc/traefik/traefik.yml"
    volumes:
      - ./src/configs/traefik/traefik.yml:/etc/traefik/traefik.yml:ro
      - ./src/configs/traefik/dynamic.yml:/etc/traefik/dynamic.yml:ro
    ports:
      - "${WEB_SERVER_PORT}:80"

  frontend:
    <<: [ *common-networks, *common-restart ]
    container_name: telepy-nextjs-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    build:
      context: ./src/frontend
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
      args:
        NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID:-}
    environment:
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE=
      - NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=${SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID:-}

  # 後端：單一 Rust 程序 = REST + WebSocket + 內建 SSH gateway（裝置的反向隧道直接接到這裡）+
  # 狀態/延遲監控 + remote-browser session。沒有 supervisor、redis、ssh 容器。
  # Backend: one Rust process serving REST, WebSockets, the SSH gateway that terminates the devices'
  # reverse tunnels, the status/latency monitor and remote-browser sessions.
  backend:
    <<: [ *common-networks, *common-restart ]
    build:
      context: ./src/backend-api
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    image: telepy-server
    hostname: telepy-web-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    container_name: telepy-web-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    environment:
      - DEBUG=${DEBUG}
      # 下面標 [Server] 的變數都是選用的：沒設（空）= 用「網站設定 → 伺服器」存的值；有設就以這裡為準並鎖住那一格。
      # 所以預設一律留空，不要寫 `:-true` 之類的預設值。
      # Variables marked [Server] are optional: unset (empty) = the value saved under Site settings → Server; a value
      # here wins and locks that field. So they default to empty here — never `:-true` or similar.
      # [Server] log level.
      - LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-}
      # [Server] Swagger UI (/api/__hidden_swagger) + OpenAPI spec (/api/openapi.json), logged-in users only.
      - OPENAPI_ENABLED=${OPENAPI_ENABLED:-}
      # JWT 簽章金鑰；留空沿用舊版 Django 的預設（啟動時會警告）。正式環境請設定。
      # JWT signing key; empty keeps the legacy default (warned at startup). Set it in production.
      - SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY:-}
      - REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT=${REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT}
      - WEB_SERVER_PORT=${WEB_SERVER_PORT}
      # [Server]
      - SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=${SOCIAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID:-}
      - SERVER_DOMAIN=${SERVER_DOMAIN}
      - SSH_SERVER_DOMAIN=${SSH_SERVER_DOMAIN:-}
      # [Server] 對外 base URL（MCP 連接器的 OAuth issuer）；留空依網站設定，再沒有就依 X-Forwarded-* 推導。
      # [Server] Public base URL (the OAuth issuer); empty = the site setting, else from the request.
      - PUBLIC_URL=${PUBLIC_URL:-}
      # 使用者來源 IP（登入紀錄 / 誰在用通道）：auto = X-Forwarded-For 右邊的內部位址都算代理（Traefik、前面的
      # Nginx Proxy Manager），不必數層數；數字 = 固定跳過幾層（含 Traefik）。
      # Client IP: auto = every internal address at the right of X-Forwarded-For is a proxy (Traefik, an upstream
      # Nginx Proxy Manager), nothing to count; a number = skip exactly that many, Traefik included.
      # [Server] 空 = 網站設定（預設 auto）。/ Empty = the site setting (default auto).
      - TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS=${TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS:-}
      - CLIENT_IP_HEADER=${CLIENT_IP_HEADER:-}
      - INTERNAL_API_TOKEN=${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN}
      - KASM_BROWSER_API=http://kasm-browser:7000
      - KASM_BROWSER_HOST=kasm-browser
      # KasmVNC web 層 Basic Auth 帳密(consumer 帶去連上游 ws;與 kasm-browser 的 build args 同源)。
      - KASM_WS_USER=${KASM_WS_USER:-telepy}
      - KASM_WS_PASSWORD=${KASM_WS_PASSWORD:-telepyvnc}
      # 遠端桌面（RDP / VNC）引擎 guacd 的位址，以及 guacd 連回 backend 時用的名字（兩者都在 telepy-desktop 網路上）。
      # Remote desktop engine (guacd) and the name it dials back to (both on the telepy-desktop network).
      - GUACD_ADDR=guacd:4822
      - DESKTOP_CALLBACK_HOST=backend
      # 內建 SSH gateway：沿用原本的 host keys，裝置端 known_hosts 不受影響；資料夾是空的就在第一次啟動時產生。
      # In-process SSH gateway; reuses the existing host keys so devices see the same host identity. An empty folder is
      # filled with new keys on the first start.
      - GATEWAY_HOST_KEYS_DIR=/config/ssh_host_keys
      # 後端登入裝置用的服務金鑰（私鑰）；不存在就在第一次啟動時產生，公鑰在旁邊的 .pub。
      # The service key the backend logs in to devices with; created on the first start when missing.
      - SSH_IDENTITY=/root/.ssh/id_rsa
      # gateway 前面有 L4 代理（nginx stream / HAProxy / NLB）時填它的 IP / CIDR，讓它送 PROXY protocol header 帶出裝置真正的 IP。
      # [Server] IPs / CIDRs of an L4 proxy in front of the gateway that sends a PROXY protocol header (the device's real IP).
      - GATEWAY_PROXY_PROTOCOL_FROM=${GATEWAY_PROXY_PROTOCOL_FROM:-}
      # [Server] 裝置連上時登入問一次它的 hostname / 內網 / 公網 IP（false 關閉）。/ Ask each device for its addresses once per connection.
      - DEVICE_PROBE=${DEVICE_PROBE:-}
      # [Server] 共用服務金鑰留在裝置上（另一台 Telepy 還用它登入時，例如並行的舊站）。/ Keep the shared service key on devices.
      - KEEP_SHARED_SERVICE_KEY=${KEEP_SHARED_SERVICE_KEY:-}
      # 離線 IP 地理資料庫 / 網卡廠商表放在容器裡的哪裡（空 = /data/geoip、/data/oui；
      # `docker compose exec backend telepy-server geoip` / `oui` 會下載到那裡）。
      # Where the backend reads the IP geolocation databases / NIC vendor list (container paths; empty = /data/geoip,
      # /data/oui, which `docker compose exec backend telepy-server geoip` / `oui` fill).
      - GEOIP_DIR=${GEOIP_DIR:-}
      - OUI_DIR=${OUI_DIR:-}
    volumes:
      # Mutable data (SQLite db)
      - ./telepy-data:/data
      # Logging (telepy.log / error.log / ssh-gateway.log)
      - ./telepy-logs/backend:/logs
      # SSH: backend client key (service key) + ssh config
      - ./ssh/backend_ssh_key:/root/.ssh
      # SSH gateway host keys (the backend creates missing ones at start, so the mount is writable)
      - ./ssh/ssh_host_keys:/config/ssh_host_keys
    ports:
      # 裝置的反向 SSH 連線：REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT → 內建 gateway。
      # Devices' reverse SSH connections land on the in-process gateway.
      - ${REVERSE_SERVER_SSH_PORT}:2222
    # 健康檢查：打公開的輕量端點（只數一次 User）。schema 補齊在 listen 之前完成，通常 <1s。
    # Health via a cheap public endpoint; schema reconciliation runs before listening.
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://localhost:8000/api/auth/setup-status"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 15s
    # telepy-desktop：只有 backend 與 guacd（guacd 沒有認證，不讓其他容器碰得到）。
    # telepy-desktop holds only the backend and guacd (guacd has no authentication).
    networks:
      - telepy-network
      - telepy-desktop
    depends_on:
      - kasm-browser
      - guacd

  # 共用 KasmVNC 瀏覽器容器(取代 CDP 的 chromium)。內含 KasmVNC + Chromium + CJK 字型 +
  # 一支 session-manager API(:7000)。backend 呼叫它 per-session 起 Xvnc+chromium(注入該
  # session 的 SOCKS proxy),回傳 RFB 埠;後端把該 RFB 埠橋接到既有 /ws。
  # session-manager(7000)與各 session 的 RFB 埠(5910+)只在 telepy-network 內,絕不 publish。
  # 首次或改版需 build:docker compose up -d --build kasm-browser
  # Shared KasmVNC browser container: KasmVNC + Chromium + CJK fonts + a session-manager API.
  # Per session it starts Xkasmvnc + chromium (with that session's SOCKS proxy) and returns the
  # websocket port; the backend WS↔WS-relays it to the existing /ws. Nothing is published.
  kasm-browser:
    <<: [ *common-networks, *common-restart ]
    # tini 當 PID 1:回收被 reparent 的孤兒(chromium 關閉/respawn 會留 zombie,
    # session-manager 自己不 reap 非親生子行程),並轉發 SIGTERM 讓 graceful stop 照常。
    init: true
    build:
      context: ./docker/kasm-browser
      args:
        # Basic Auth 使用者(與 backend 的 KASM_WS_USER/PASSWORD 同源,單一 .env 控制)。
        KASMVNC_USER: ${KASM_WS_USER:-telepy}
        KASMVNC_PASSWORD: ${KASM_WS_PASSWORD:-telepyvnc}
        # KasmVNC 版本可覆寫:KASMVNC_VERSION: "1.4.0"
    image: telepy-kasm-browser:latest
    container_name: telepy-kasm-browser-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    hostname: telepy-kasm-browser-${PROJECT_NAME:-main}
    shm_size: "2gb"                 # chromium 需要較大的 /dev/shm
    environment:
      # session-manager 用此 token 驗證只有 backend 能起/停 session(與 backend 同一把)。
      - INTERNAL_API_TOKEN=${INTERNAL_API_TOKEN}
      - SESSION_MANAGER_PORT=7000
      # 遠端瀏覽器:首頁與語系(反爬蟲:語系會影響 navigator.languages / Accept-Language)。
      - REMOTE_BROWSER_HOMEPAGE=${REMOTE_BROWSER_HOMEPAGE:-https://www.google.com}
      - REMOTE_BROWSER_LANG=${REMOTE_BROWSER_LANG:-zh-TW}
    # 瀏覽器設定檔:每 session 臨時目錄、停止即刪(不保留歷史),故不掛任何 volume。
    # 不 publish 任何埠:只在 telepy-network 內 / never published to host

  # 遠端桌面引擎：guacd 把 RDP / VNC 轉成 Guacamole 協定，backend 中繼到瀏覽器（guacamole-common-js）。
  # 每個 session guacd 連回 backend 上一個一次性的埠，backend 再把它接到裝置 sshd 的 direct-tcpip 通道，
  # 所以 guacd 碰不到任何裝置，只在 internal 網路上，沒有對外埠。
  # Remote desktop engine. Per session it dials a one-shot port on the backend, which pipes it into a

# neo-agent-skills

The canonical agent skill substrate for the `neomjs` organization. Consuming repositories **depend
on this package**; they never carry a copy of it.

## How it reaches a repository

```bash
npm install --save-dev neo-agent-skills
```

Then run the materializer from your `postinstall`:

```json
{
  "scripts": { "postinstall": "neo-agent-skills-materialize" },
  "devDependencies": { "neo-agent-skills": "^0.1.0" }
}
```

`postinstall` materializes **two surfaces**, both as symlinks into `node_modules`, both untracked:

| surface | shape | for |
|---|---|---|
| `.agents/skills` | **one directory symlink** at the whole tree | harness-neutral discovery — Codex, Antigravity, any fork |
| `.claude/skills` | **per-skill links**, manifest-projected | the Claude façade |

The shapes differ on purpose. The manifest may opt a skill out of the Claude façade, and **you cannot
opt a skill out of a directory symlink** — so the neutral surface links the tree and the façade links
each skill. Git-ignore both paths; a tracked entry under either is a shadow copy, which is the thing
this package exists to make unnecessary.

**A workspace that is not ours projects one audience.** `neo-agent-skills-materialize --audience app`
(and `--check --audience app`) links only the skills whose manifest row lists `app` — today
`neo-app-authoring` and `neural-link` — and both surfaces become per-skill links, because a directory
link would expose the maintainer corpus. `neo-app` passes the flag from the workspaces it creates; the
audience is declared by the caller, never inferred. A row without `audiences` serves maintainers, so the
projection without the flag is unchanged. The matching instruction file comes from
`neo-agent-skills-agents-md --repo neo-app-workspace --audience app`.

**Maintainer pull requests bump this package's version and publish on merge. Dependabot pull requests
retain the package version and run validation without publishing or tagging** (see *Authority*).
Consumers update the dependency like any other.
Freshness is whatever npm already tells you — `npm outdated`, dependabot — and there is deliberately
no bespoke lag gate anywhere in this contract.

## The check that matters

```bash
npx neo-agent-skills-materialize --check
```

Run it in consumer CI. It answers the questions this transport leaves open: **did both projections happen, and does every
link point where it should?** Existence is not correctness — a link resolving to the wrong skill
resolves.

It can silently not happen. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` skips `postinstall` *and* `prepare`, and is
already deliberate practice in several `neomjs` workflows — that yields a resolved dependency and
zero reachable skills. A dependency resolving is not the same as skills being reachable, and only
this check tells them apart.

One measured npm behaviour worth knowing: **`npm install <pkg>` does not run your `postinstall`;
a bare `npm install` does.** So the command that bumps this dependency leaves the links stale until
the next install. `--check` is what turns that from silent into loud.

## Shared source-comment guard

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-ticket-archaeology --base origin/dev
```

The guard scans every changed tracked `.mjs` file in full. Repository-local issue numbers of any
length and review-history markers fail only in comments or JSDoc; executable strings remain valid.
A numeric CSS color of 3, 4, 6 or 8 digits passes directly after color syntax (`color:`,
`backgroundColor_=`, `fillStyle=`, `CSS color`), a number with a leading zero is never a ticket, and a
numeric HTML entity (`'`) is a codepoint rather than a reference;
anywhere else a bare number stays a ref. A token-scoped `[not-ticket-ref: …]` marker binds to the one
token it follows: `css-color` on such a color, or any other non-blank reason on a numeric reference
the author declares deliberate. A marker binding to neither, or carrying no reason, fails closed.
Consumer repositories call the stable `Source comment archaeology` job in
`.github/workflows/reusable-pr-baseline.yml` at a published release tag (`@vX.Y.Z`): its `Release ref` job fails
a caller at a SHA or a branch, and every publish pushes the matching tag. That job installs
its exact guard release outside the caller workspace, so a pull request cannot weaken its own gate by
changing the caller lockfile or local binary.

## Shared substrate byte-budget guard

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-substrate-size
```

Measures what a seat actually **loads** per turn — `AGENTS.md`, `.agents/ANTIGRAVITY_RULES.md`,
`.claude/CLAUDE.md` — against a **23,800-byte** per-file limit, and fails the check on a breach.

Loaded bytes, not file bytes: symlinks resolve through `realpathSync` (an `lstat` on a symlinked
`CLAUDE.md` reports **12** — the length of `../AGENTS.md`), and whole-line `@path` imports are summed
recursively as one unit with a cycle guard keyed on file identity. It reports **headroom** rather than
pass/fail, because this drift is gradual: by the time a file flips to EXCEEDS it is already truncating.

**Past the limit the harness silently truncates the BOTTOM of the file**, so a seat loses the tail of
its own rules with nothing reporting it — the one failure that cannot be observed from inside the seat
suffering it.

**A missing entry point is `not applicable`, never a failure.** Consumers legitimately differ: only
some carry all three. **Only `ENOENT` means absent** — a permission denial or an unreadable path is an
error and fails the check, because absent is a claim about the repository while unreadable is a claim
about the observation, and a failed observation supports neither.

Consumer repositories call the stable `Substrate size` job in
`.github/workflows/reusable-pr-baseline.yml` at a published release tag (`@vX.Y.Z`). **The limit ships
with the guard, not with the caller**: the job installs its exact release outside the caller workspace
and pins the measurement to the checked-out tree, so a pull request cannot widen the limit it is judged
by, drop an entry from the target roster, or move the measurement to a directory where every target is
absent and the check greens on nothing.

## Shared npm-overrides guard

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-npm-overrides
```

An npm `overrides` rule is a floor: it keeps a dependent whose declared range still admits a
vulnerable version from resolving beneath the patched one. **Dependabot neither bumps nor removes
`overrides`**, so a rule outlives its reason silently. Worse, when a dependent moves to a new major,
the stale rule forces it back onto the old one.

The guard judges each rule against the ranges its dependents **declare** in `package-lock.json`, with
no network. A nested rule (`"parent": {"pkg": …}`) counts only dependents inside `parent`'s
resolved subtree, hoisted ones included:

| verdict | meaning |
|---|---|
| `needed` | a dependent in scope still admits a version below the floor; the offending ranges are printed |
| `REDUNDANT` | nothing in scope can resolve below the floor, or nothing declares the package any more: delete the rule |
| `FIGHTING` | a dependent's range starts above everything the rule permits: delete or raise the rule, or narrow it when another dependent still needs the floor |

Holding a package above an exact pin (`dompurify: "3.4.8"` held at `^3.4.13`) is the deliberate
security direction, so it reads `needed`. No `overrides` is N/A. A missing `package.json`, or
overrides with no v2/v3 lock, is a failed observation and exits 1.

Consumer repositories call the stable `npm overrides` job in `.github/workflows/reusable-pr-baseline.yml`.
The verdict can only change in a pull request that edits `package.json` or `package-lock.json`, so
the job runs on every pull request and never reddens one for an upstream release.

## Shared credential guard

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-secrets --all
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-secrets path/to/file.mjs other/file.md
```

A committed credential is unrecallable one `npm publish` later, and a scanner that finds it after
the push finds it too late. This guard knows Google API keys and OAuth tokens, OpenAI, Anthropic and
GitHub tokens (classic and fine-grained), and AWS access key ids. Each pattern is anchored to the
credential's real length, so prose that describes one (`AIza…`, a placeholder, a short sample) passes.

**A finding names file, line and kind, never the match**: CI logs are published, and echoing a
finding would publish it.

A line that must keep such a literal carries `secret-scan-ok: <reason>` in whatever comment syntax
the file has. The reason runs to the end of the line or to the comment's closer, and it has to say
something: `<!-- secret-scan-ok: -->` is a finding, because a closer is no reason, and so is the
credential itself written after the marker. A marker covers its own line only.

Consumer repositories call the stable `Secrets` job in `.github/workflows/reusable-pr-baseline.yml`. It
scans **every tracked file** at the pull request's head, not only the diff: a credential already on
the base branch still fails, because it is one to revoke whichever pull request finds it.

## Shared PR-review check

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-pr-review-body --envelope review.json --json --comment-file comment.md
```

```js
import {judgeReview} from 'neo-agent-skills/pr-review-policy';
```

Brain's `manage_pr_review` refuses a malformed agent review before it posts. A review submitted with
`gh pr review` or in the UI skips that gate, so consumer repositories call
`.github/workflows/reusable-pr-review.yml` on `pull_request_review` and get the same policy afterwards: a
red `Review body` check and one corrective comment per failing review, edited in place when the review
is. The check is informative, not required: it runs once per review, so a new head has no result until
the next one.

The policy ships beside the templates it enforces, so one release carries both. A diagnostic names at
most one missing anchor and never a structural one. The bin exits 0 on a pass or on a review that is
not an agent's, 1 on a policy failure, and 2 on a malformed envelope.

## Generated `AGENTS.md`

```bash
npx --no-install neo-agent-skills-agents-md --repo neo,neo-agent-brain --out AGENTS.md
```

```js
import {generate} from 'neo-agent-skills/agents-md';

const {text} = generate({audience: 'maintainer', repos: ['neo', 'neo-agent-brain']});
```

The instructions a seat loads every turn are composed from `agents-md/sections/`. Each section declares
the repositories and the audience (`maintainer` or `contributor`) it applies to; nothing is inferred. A
set of repositories composes one file, with every section once, in source order, when any repository
in the set declares it. A peer working in several repositories loads that one file and keeps each
repository's own rules.

Both callers get the same refusals: an undeclared repository or audience, two sections claiming one
numbered rule, and output over the **23,800-byte** budget. The bin writes `--out`, or stdout. The
import writes nothing: Fleet puts the text into each seat's harness home with its own safe write.

## What is in the package

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `.agents/skills/` | the substrate — skills plus `skills.manifest.json` and its schema |
| `scripts/materialize-harness-skills.mjs` | the postinstall linker and its `--check` arm |
| `scripts/check-ticket-archaeology.mjs` | the portable comment/JSDoc archaeology guard |
| `scripts/check-npm-overrides.mjs` | the portable stale-`overrides` guard |
| `scripts/check-substrate-size.mjs` | the portable per-turn substrate byte-budget guard |
| `scripts/check-pr-review-body.mjs` | the agent PR-review policy (`./pr-review-policy`) and its bin |

The manifest governs **projection**: a skill declaring `claudeSymlinkRequired: false` is a declared
opt-out and is correctly absent from the façade. Per-skill links rather than one directory link,
because a skill cannot be opted out of a directory symlink.

## Authority

Skills are authored on `dev`:
- maintainer pull requests bump `package.json`; Dependabot keeps the base version (`scripts/check-version-bump.mjs`);
- both run validation; `.github/workflows/publish.yml` classifies the exact merged PR's author, so a human merging Dependabot cannot turn it into a release;
- maintainer merges publish through npm trusted publishing and push `v<version>`; Dependabot merges do neither;
- Dependabot brings it to each consumer.

**A repository's Dependabot pull requests merge themselves.** Its caller of `reusable-dependabot-automerge.yml` hands
every pull request Dependabot opens to GitHub's auto-merge, majors included, unless the caller narrows
`dependency_allow_list` or `update_types`. Before arming, the workflow reads the repository live: *Allow auto-merge*
on, at least one required status check in the base branch's rulesets, and the head still the admitted commit. A failed
read turns the run red and arms nothing. GitHub then merges once the **required** checks pass, so the ruleset decides
what green means. Each later event decides again, and one another account sent takes the arming back, so a fix a peer
pushes never merges this way. No agent merges: critical gate 1's `machine_merge` line names this one machine path. The
operator sets *Allow auto-merge* and the ruleset's required checks per repository. The repository variable
`NEO_AUTOMERGE_DEPENDABOT=off` stops new armings and takes each armed one back at its next event.

Dependabot changes to shipped dependency declarations or reusable workflows are included in the
next maintainer release. Lock-only updates refresh repository validation; consumers resolve
dependencies through their own lockfiles.

The version is written once, in `package.json`, and read everywhere else. **The package version, the registry
tarball integrity, and the consumer's lockfile are the revision authority.** There is no receipt file; an earlier design used
one to police byte-copies across repositories, and both the copies and the receipt are gone.

- Dependabot brings it to each consumer.

**A repository's Dependabot pull requests merge themselves.** Its caller of `reusable-dependabot-automerge.yml` hands
every pull request Dependabot opens to GitHub's auto-merge, majors included, unless the caller narrows
`dependency_allow_list` or `update_types`. Before arming, the workflow reads the repository live: *Allow auto-merge*
on, at least one required status check in the base branch's rulesets, and the head still the admitted commit. A failed
read turns the run red and arms nothing. GitHub then merges once the **required** checks pass, so the ruleset decides
what green means. Each later event decides again, and one another account sent takes the arming back, so a fix a peer
pushes never merges this way. No agent merges: critical gate 1's `machine_merge` line names this one machine path. The
operator sets *Allow auto-merge* and the ruleset's required checks per repository. The repository variable
`NEO_AUTOMERGE_DEPENDABOT=off` stops new armings and takes each armed one back at its next event.

Dependabot changes to shipped dependency declarations or reusable workflows are included in the
next maintainer release. Lock-only updates refresh repository validation; consumers resolve
dependencies through their own lockfiles.

The version is written once, in `package.json`, and read everywhere else. **The package version, the registry
tarball integrity, and the consumer's lockfile are the revision authority.** There is no receipt file; an earlier design used
one to police byte-copies across repositories, and both the copies and the receipt are gone.
